turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Dr. [Name]. Um, well, I guess I'm here because... people keep telling me they can't follow what I'm trying to explain anymore. Like, my artist statements and my client notes, or even just what I say in meetings. I'll be talking and I just start jumping around from the textures of the materials, straight into the budgets, and then into the secret meanings behind the pieces. 

Which, honestly, the secret meanings are the most important part. I was actually reading this article the other day about Renaissance painters and how they hid all these codes in the folds of the clothing they painted. Did you know that? They used lapis lazuli for the blue, which was so expensive they had to budget for it separately. Which kind of reminds me of how expensive groceries are getting right now. I went to buy avocados yesterday and they were almost three dollars each, it's just ridiculous. 

But, um... yeah, my clients and the gallery people just look at me like they have no idea what I'm talking about when I try to explain my work.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient reports that others cannot follow their explanations because they jump between unrelated topics, and they demonstrate tangential speech during the response by drifting from art to Renaissance painters, lapis lazuli, and the price of avocados.

turns.doctor_question: When did you first notice that people started having trouble following what you're saying? Was this something that started suddenly over days or weeks, or has it been going on for much longer?
turns.patient_response:
Um, it wasn't sudden. It's been going on for a while now, I'd say about a year and two months? Yeah, it started right around the time I switched from community curation into full-time independent installation work. 

Community curation was just so exhausting, honestly. You have to deal with so many different personalities and local government grants. I remember this one grant application required a fifty-page proposal just to get funding for a neighborhood sculpture garden. And the paper they printed the forms on was that awful, cheap recycled paper that just drinks the ink right out of your pen. It bleeds everywhere. I only use archival ink now for my own sketches. It's waterproof, which is super important because I actually spilled coffee on my sketchbook last week and it almost ruined this drawing I was doing of a... 

Wait, I'm sorry. I lost my train of thought. But yeah, about fourteen months, ever since I went independent.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient actively demonstrates disorganized thinking and tangential speech by drifting from the timeline of their symptoms to job details, grant applications, paper quality, ink types, and spilling coffee, before ultimately losing their train of thought.

turns.doctor_question: Over this past year or so, have you been feeling unusually energetic, confident, or like you need less sleep than normal? Or has your mood felt pretty much like it always does?
turns.patient_response:
Um, yeah, I guess so. There are definitely these stretches where I just feel completely lit up, you know? Like I'm almost unstoppable and every single idea I have is just brilliant. I'll be working in the studio and it feels like the universe is just pouring inspiration straight into my hands. Which is funny, because I was reading about how the ancient Greeks believed in Muses, like actual entities that would come down and whisper ideas to you. I think there were nine of them? One was for astronomy, which is so interesting because I've been looking at star charts lately. The patterns are just incredible, especially if you map them out using silver leaf on dark canvas. Silver leaf is so tricky to work with, though. If you even breathe too hard, it just flies away and gets stuck to everything. I found a piece of it on my cat's nose the other day, and she just looked so regal, like a little Egyptian statue. 

But, um, where was I? Oh, right, the energy. Yeah, I get super energetic and confident, but then... I don't know, sometimes it flips. Like, a collaborator will make just a tiny comment about a piece, something really small, and I'll just snap at them. It feels way bigger than the situation warrants, just this intense irritation that bubbles up out of nowhere.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from inspiration to Greek Muses, astronomy, silver leaf, and their cat before losing their train of thought.
symptom_reasoning.S033: The patient describes periods of feeling 'completely lit up' as well as experiencing 'intense irritation' that bubbles up.
symptom_reasoning.S034: The patient explicitly confirms getting 'super energetic' during these stretches.
symptom_reasoning.S035: The patient describes feeling 'almost unstoppable' and believing that 'every single idea I have is just brilliant.'
symptom_reasoning.S060: The patient admits to snapping at collaborators over tiny comments, demonstrating snappiness and reacting sharply to minor stimuli.

turns.doctor_question: When you're in one of those 'lit up' energetic periods, how long does it typically last before your mood shifts or returns to normal? Are we talking hours, days, weeks, or longer?
turns.patient_response:
Um, it's usually weeks. I'd say these energized stretches where I'm barely sleeping and just juggling way too many projects, and getting so irritable—that's been happening for about 10 months now. It's like I get locked into this high gear for weeks on end. 

Which reminds me, I actually started a new project last month that involves weaving different types of copper wire. Copper is so fascinating because of how it oxidizes. It turns that beautiful green color, like the Statue of Liberty. I visited New York once when I was in college, and the ferry ride over there was so windy I lost my favorite hat. It was this vintage wool fedora I found at a thrift store in Portland. Portland has the best thrift stores, honestly. I found this amazing mid-century modern lamp there once, but the wiring was totally shot, so I had to learn how to rewire it myself watching YouTube videos. The guy in the video had this really soothing voice, kind of like a late-night radio DJ. 

But, um... yeah, those high-energy periods definitely last for weeks at a time.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech and loose associations, drifting from copper wire to the Statue of Liberty, a lost hat, Portland thrift stores, and a YouTube video.
symptom_reasoning.S033: The patient explicitly mentions getting 'so irritable' during these periods.
symptom_reasoning.S034: The patient describes experiencing 'energized stretches' and feeling 'locked into this high gear.'
symptom_reasoning.S036: The patient states they are 'barely sleeping' during these high-energy periods.

turns.doctor_question: When you're not in one of those high-energy, barely-sleeping periods, what is your mood like? Do you experience periods where you feel depressed, down, or low?
turns.patient_response:
Um, no, not really. I mean, I don't think I get depressed or down. When I'm not in that crazy high gear, I just feel kind of regular, I guess? Like, just normal. Which is nice, actually, because being normal means I can just sit and focus on mixing paints without feeling like I have to paint the entire room. 

I've been experimenting with mixing my own pigments lately, actually. You can buy these raw pigment powders online, and you mix them with a binder, like linseed oil or walnut oil. Walnut oil dries a lot slower, which gives you more time to work, but it smells so earthy. It reminds me of this hiking trail near my childhood home. We used to go there every autumn, and the ground would just be covered in these crushed black walnuts. They stain your hands this deep, dark brown if you touch them. My brother used to throw them at me, and I'd have stained hands for a week, which was so embarrassing in middle school. Middle school was just the worst anyway, wasn't it? Everyone is so awkward and trying to figure out who they are. I wore these terrible neon shoelaces for a whole year thinking it was a fashion statement. 

But, um... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, feeling low. Yeah, no, I haven't really noticed feeling depressed or anything like that. Just normal.

symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient explicitly denies experiencing periods of feeling depressed, down, or low, stating they just feel 'normal' when not in a high-energy state.

turns.doctor_question: When you're in those normal periods between the high-energy weeks, have you ever noticed times where your mood goes noticeably lower than normal—like feeling sad, hopeless, or having much less interest in things you usually enjoy?
turns.patient_response:
Um, no, like I said, I don't really get sad or hopeless. When the energy stops, I'm just back to baseline, you know? Just my regular self. It's actually a relief sometimes because I can finally just sit still and read a book. I've been reading this massive biography of Frida Kahlo, actually. Her life was so intense, especially with the bus accident and everything. It's amazing how she channeled all that physical pain into her self-portraits. I tried doing a self-portrait once, but I could never get the nose right. Noses are the hardest part of the face to draw, I swear. The shading is just so subtle. You have to get the light hitting the bridge exactly right or it looks completely flat. I took this life drawing class in college where the professor made us draw the same nose for three hours straight. He was this really eccentric guy who always wore a beret, like a literal beret, indoors. Who even does that anymore? But he did teach me a lot about charcoal. Charcoal is so messy, though. You get it all over your hands and then you accidentally touch your face and you look like a chimney sweep. 

But, um... yeah, no sadness or anything like that. Just regular me.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from reading a book to Frida Kahlo, drawing noses, a college professor, and charcoal before returning to the original topic.
symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient explicitly denies experiencing sadness, stating 'I don't really get sad' and 'no sadness or anything like that.'
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient denies the doctor's question about losing interest in activities and mentions enjoying reading books during these periods.
symptom_reasoning.S083: The patient explicitly denies feeling hopeless.

turns.doctor_question: I want to make sure I'm not missing anything. During those weeks when you're back to your normal baseline—the times when you're not in that high-energy state—have you ever had a period where your mood actually dipped below normal? Like feeling persistently sad, empty, or noticeably losing interest in art or other things you usually care about?
turns.patient_response:
No, really, I promise I'm not hiding anything. When I'm not going a million miles an hour, I don't feel sad or empty or whatever. I just feel like me. I still paint, I still read, I still do my stuff. I actually just started a new painting yesterday, speaking of art. It's on this huge canvas, like four feet by four feet. I had to stretch it myself, which is such a workout. You need those special canvas pliers, and if you don't pull it tight enough, it sags in the middle like a trampoline. I used to jump on my neighbor's trampoline when I was a kid. We'd put the sprinkler under it in the summer, and it was so much fun until my sister slipped and chipped her front tooth. She had to get this fake cap put on it, and it always looked just a tiny bit whiter than the rest of her teeth. She was so self-conscious about it in high school. High school was rough for her, she was always trying to fit in with the popular crowd, but they were so mean. 

But anyway, yeah, I don't get depressed. I just go back to normal.

turns.doctor_question: During those normal weeks when you're back to baseline, have you ever noticed that you're sleeping more than usual, or that you feel more tired or sluggish than your normal self—even if you're still interested in your art?
turns.patient_response:
Um, sleeping more? Not really. I mean, maybe a normal amount, like eight hours? When I'm in the high-energy weeks I barely sleep at all, so I guess compared to that it seems like a lot, but it's just regular sleeping. I don't feel sluggish or anything. I actually really like the mornings when I'm at my baseline. I make this pour-over coffee, which takes forever but it's totally worth it. You have to get the water temperature exactly right, like 205 degrees, or it burns the beans and gets all bitter. I bought this gooseneck kettle just for it. It looks like a magic lamp or something. I almost brought it to a thrift store last month because I was going through this huge minimalism phase, trying to declutter my whole apartment. I watched all those videos about only keeping things that spark joy, but then I realized basically all my art supplies spark joy, so I couldn't get rid of any of it. My closet is just overflowing with sketchbooks. I have sketchbooks from when I was like, twelve. There's this one where I tried to draw horses, but their legs look like hot dogs. It's so embarrassing. 

But yeah, my sleep is fine. I just wake up and make my coffee.

But um, no, I wouldn't say I do anything dangerous or get into trouble. Just... maybe buying too many canvases sometimes.

turns.doctor_question: During those high-energy weeks when you're barely sleeping, do you actually feel rested and energized on just a few hours of sleep, or do you feel tired but just can't seem to sleep?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, I definitely feel rested. It's actually amazing. Like, I can be up working on a piece until three in the morning, sleep for maybe two or three hours, and then I just pop awake. I feel completely bright and ready to keep going, not tired at all like I normally would be if I only got three hours. It's like my body just doesn't need it. I actually love that feeling because the mornings are so quiet. The light coming through my studio window is perfect right around 6 AM. It's this really cool, bluish light that makes all the colors on my palette look totally different. I was trying to mix this specific shade of cerulean blue the other day, and I realized I was out of titanium white, which is a disaster because you literally use titanium white for everything. I prefer the heavy body acrylics because they hold their texture so well, you know? You can get those really thick, impasto strokes that look almost like frosting. I tried baking a cake once and tried to frost it like a painting, using a palette knife and everything. It was a lemon cake. My grandmother used to make the best lemon cake, she had this secret ingredient which turned out to be just a little bit of sour cream in the batter, which keeps it super moist. 

But yeah, I don't feel tired at all during those weeks. Just energized and ready to go.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates tangentiality, drifting from the topic of morning light to mixing paint, then to frosting a cake, and finally to their grandmother's lemon cake recipe.
